questions.text: The basic consumer-choice model says that a consumer chooses

options.a: the bundle with the largest x1-intercept.
options.b: the bundle with the lowest total expenditure regardless of preferences.
options.c: the most preferred bundle in the budget set.
options.d: the bundle containing equal quantities of both goods.

questions.text: Equivalently, consumer choice can be formulated as

options.a: maximizing prices subject to demand.
options.b: equalizing all quantities regardless of prices.
options.c: minimizing income subject to a production function.
options.d: maximizing utility subject to the budget constraint.

questions.text: With monotonic preferences, an optimal bundle typically lies on the budget line because

options.a: if income were left unspent, more of at least one good could be purchased and would be preferred.
options.b: the budget set contains only its boundary.
options.c: the budget line is always an indifference curve.
options.d: utility is independent of quantities inside the budget set.

questions.text: For a smooth interior optimum with well-behaved preferences, a necessary tangency condition is

options.a: MRS = p1 + p2.
options.b: MRS = −p1/p2.
options.c: MU1 = MU2 regardless of prices.
options.d: x1 = x2 regardless of preferences.

questions.text: Why can the tangency condition fail at a kinked optimum?

options.a: Kinked preferences are necessarily incomplete.
options.b: The indifference curve may not have a unique tangent at the kink.
options.c: Prices are undefined at a kink.
options.d: The budget constraint is absent.

questions.text: Why can the tangency condition fail at a boundary optimum?

options.a: The consumer must have negative income.
options.b: The budget line is horizontal at all boundary points.
options.c: A boundary optimum is never utility maximizing.
options.d: The optimum may occur where one good is consumed in zero quantity, so the budget line need not be tangent to an indifference curve.

questions.text: For convex preferences, a tangency point between a smooth indifference curve and the budget line is

options.a: never an optimum.
options.b: sufficient only when preferences are concave.
options.c: necessarily unique even with flat indifference-curve segments.
options.d: sufficient for an optimum, though multiple optima can still occur with flat spots.

questions.text: Strictly convex preferences imply that, on a given budget line, the consumer has

options.a: only boundary optima.
options.b: no utility-maximizing bundle.
options.c: a unique optimal bundle.
options.d: infinitely many optimal bundles.

questions.text: At an interior optimum, equality of MRS and the price ratio means that

options.a: the two market prices must be equal.
options.b: the consumer is indifferent to all affordable bundles.
options.c: marginal utilities must both be zero.
options.d: the consumer’s marginal willingness to trade the goods equals the market’s rate of exchange.

questions.text: If the consumer’s MRS differs from −p1/p2 at an interior bundle, then

options.a: the budget constraint cannot bind.
options.b: the bundle cannot be optimal because a feasible reallocation can improve utility.
options.c: the bundle must be the unique optimum.
options.d: the consumer is necessarily at a satiation point.

questions.text: A Marshallian demand function gives

options.a: the utility level as a function of quantities only.
options.b: the market supply of the good as a function of wages.
options.c: the production cost of the good.
options.d: the utility-maximizing quantity of a good as a function of prices and income.

questions.text: Different preferences can generate different demand functions because

options.a: the optimal bundle depends on how the consumer ranks affordable bundles.
options.b: preferences determine the budget line’s slope.
options.c: prices have no role in demand.
options.d: income is irrelevant to all consumers.

questions.text: For one-for-one perfect substitutes with u=x1+x2, if p1 < p2, the consumer will generally

options.a: spend all income on good 2.
options.b: buy equal physical quantities of both goods.
options.c: spend all income on good 1.
options.d: buy zero of both goods.

questions.text: For one-for-one perfect substitutes with p1 = p2, the consumer

options.a: must buy only good 2.
options.b: is indifferent among all budget-line bundles.
options.c: has no feasible bundle.
options.d: must buy only good 1.

questions.text: For perfect complements u=min(x1,x2), the utility-maximizing bundle satisfies

options.a: x1 = x2 and p1x1 + p2x2 = m.
options.b: MU1/p1 = 0 for both goods.
options.d: x1 = 0 regardless of prices.

questions.text: For u=min(x1,x2), Marshallian demand is

options.c: x1=m/p1 and x2=m/p2 simultaneously.

questions.text: If good 2 is a bad and good 1 is a desirable good, the consumer with monotonic preferences over good 1 will generally choose

options.a: the maximum possible amount of the bad.
options.b: x2 = 0 and spend available income on good 1.
options.c: only good 2.
options.d: equal quantities of the good and the bad.

questions.text: For a discrete good, demand may change only when price crosses

options.a: a reservation-price threshold at which the consumer becomes indifferent between adjacent integer quantities.
options.b: the consumer’s income exactly.
options.c: the price of the composite good only.
options.d: zero, because discrete goods cannot have positive prices.

questions.text: One way to solve a smooth interior utility-maximization problem is to combine

options.a: the price offer curve with the production function.
options.b: two different utility functions with no budget constraint.
options.c: the MRS condition with the binding budget constraint.
options.d: the supply curve with an accounting identity.

questions.text: In the substitution method, solving the budget constraint for x2 and substituting it into utility produces

options.a: a proof that the optimum is always at a corner.
options.b: a new market-equilibrium condition.
options.c: a utility function that no longer depends on prices or income.
options.d: a one-variable unconstrained maximization problem over feasible x1.

questions.text: The first-order condition from the substitution method reproduces the result that

options.a: the ratio of marginal utilities equals the price ratio at an interior optimum.
options.b: income must equal total utility.
options.c: the prices must be equal.
options.d: both marginal utilities must be zero.

questions.text: The Lagrangian for utility maximization can be written as

options.c: L = λu(x1,x2) with no budget term.
options.d: L = p1x1 + p2x2 − u(x1,x2) with no multiplier.

questions.text: The first-order conditions from the Lagrangian imply

options.a: MU1 = p2 and MU2 = p1 always.
options.b: λ = 0 for every interior optimum.
options.c: MU1 = MU2 = 0.
options.d: MU1 = λp1 and MU2 = λp2.

questions.text: At an interior optimum, MU1/p1 = MU2/p2 means that

options.a: the marginal utility per euro spent is equalized across goods.
options.b: the consumer spends the same number of euros on every good.
options.c: the quantities of all goods must be equal.
options.d: both goods must have the same price.

questions.text: The Lagrange multiplier λ on the budget constraint can be interpreted as

options.a: the consumer’s total expenditure on good 1.
options.b: the market price of utility.
options.c: the marginal utility of an additional euro of income.
options.d: the slope of the demand curve.

questions.text: For Cobb-Douglas utility u=x1^c x2^d, the Marshallian demand for good 1 is

options.d: x1 = cp1/m.

questions.text: For normalized Cobb-Douglas utility u=x1^α x2^(1−α), the consumer spends

options.a: a fraction α of income on each good.
options.b: all income on the cheaper good.
options.c: equal fractions on both goods regardless of α.
options.d: the fraction α of income on good 1 and 1−α on good 2.

questions.text: If observed expenditure shares on two goods are relatively stable across price-income situations, a natural utility specification to consider is

options.a: satiated preferences with a bliss point.
options.b: perfect substitutes with equal prices only.
options.c: Cobb-Douglas preferences.
options.d: preferences over two bads.

questions.text: If all consumers face the same prices, choose interior optima, and have well-behaved preferences, then for any two goods

options.a: their income levels must be equal.
options.b: their utility functions must be identical.
options.c: their MRS values at their chosen bundles are equal across consumers because each equals the common market price ratio.
options.d: their demanded quantities must be equal.

questions.text: Compared with a quantity tax that raises the same revenue from one consumer, a revenue-equivalent lump-sum income tax can make that consumer better off because

options.a: it makes all goods free at the margin.
options.b: it preserves the original relative price and therefore removes the substitution distortion caused by the commodity tax.
options.c: it forces the consumer to purchase the taxed bundle.
options.d: it always raises more revenue.

questions.text: A key limitation of the “income tax is better than a quantity tax” result is that

options.a: the revenue-equivalent income tax can differ across individuals and broader labor-supply and supply-side responses may matter.
options.b: the result applies only when the consumer has no budget constraint.
options.c: the result assumes quantity taxes do not change prices.
options.d: the result requires all goods to be bads.

questions.text: The indirect utility function v(p1,p2,m) gives

options.a: the market demand curve for good 1.
options.b: the maximum utility attainable at prices p1,p2 and income m.
options.c: the minimum expenditure needed to reach a fixed utility level.
options.d: utility as a function of quantities only.

questions.text: The indirect utility function can be obtained by

options.a: replacing preferences with the market supply curve.
options.b: substituting prices into the production function.
options.c: substituting Marshallian demand functions into the direct utility function.
options.d: differentiating the budget constraint with respect to utility.

questions.text: At the optimum, ∂v/∂m equals

options.c: the Lagrange multiplier λ, the marginal utility of income.
options.d: total expenditure m.

questions.text: Roy’s identity recovers Marshallian demand from the indirect utility function using

options.c: xi = pi(∂v/∂m).
options.d: xi = ∂v/∂pi + ∂v/∂m.

questions.text: Refer to the accompanying figure. What feature of the optimum is illustrated?

options.a: The consumer has perfect-complement preferences with a kinked optimum.
options.b: The optimum is a boundary solution with zero consumption of good 2, so tangency is not required.
options.c: The optimum is an interior tangency with positive quantities of both goods.
options.d: The budget line is irrelevant because the consumer is satiated.

If λ is large at the optimum, this indicates that

options.a: a small increase in income would generate a relatively large increase in maximal utility.
options.b: the consumer’s budget constraint is slack.
options.c: the consumer is necessarily at a corner solution.
options.d: all prices must be large.

questions.text: For a smooth interior optimum, the condition MU1/p1 = MU2/p2 can be understood as a “no profitable reallocation” condition because

options.a: prices no longer influence choice.
options.b: the consumer receives zero marginal utility from both goods.
options.c: the consumer must spend equal euro amounts on both goods.
options.d: moving a euro from one good to the other cannot raise utility when marginal utility per euro is already equalized.
